nodes.title: The CMS
nodes.text: The content-management system that owns the content. It is the only caller allowed to write. It tells this service what changed by POSTing events, and sends files as assets.
points: One account (the "CMS account"), several passwords may be live so one can be rotated without downtime.
It never reads the API: the CMS account gets 403 on every read route.
This service is a read model: if it were wiped, the CMS could replay its events and rebuild it.

nodes.title: Users and apps
nodes.text: Anyone who consumes the content: websites, apps, the photo library in this repository. Read-only. They see only published records that no admin has disabled, and only files the scanner has cleared.
points: A hidden record answers exactly like one that never existed (404), so the API never confirms a restricted record is there.
The photo library keeps everything in this service: photos are records, pictures are assets.

nodes.title: Admins
nodes.text: People who operate the service. They see everything (with a status), can hide a record locally without touching the CMS, and run the operational tools.
points: Every admin action is written to an append-only audit log in the same transaction as the change.
There is a test-only "erase everything" route. It exists only where it was switched on, never in Production.

nodes.title: POST /cms/events
nodes.text: The one door for content changes. The declared length is checked before a byte is read, so an oversized body is refused (413) without being transferred or held in memory.
points: Only the CMS account may call it.
A bounded number of batches are read at once; overflow gets 429 with Retry-After.
The answer is 202: stored, not yet applied.

nodes.title: PUT /cms/assets/…
nodes.text: How the CMS sends files. One PUT up to a limit, or an S3-style multipart upload: start, send parts in parallel, complete.
points: Each part may carry a SHA-256 that is checked.
Parts can be re-sent; the last one wins.
Everything goes to quarantine first.

nodes.title: GET /api/entities
nodes.text: The read API. Records come back in id order, a page at a time, by an opaque cursor, so the cost of a page does not grow with how deep you are.
points: There is deliberately no route that changes a record: the CMS is the only source of truth.
Users and admins only; the CMS account gets 403.

nodes.title: GET /api/assets/{id}
nodes.text: Downloads stream with byte ranges, so many ranges of one large file can be fetched at once and an interrupted download can resume. The ETag is the file's SHA-256.
points: Always an attachment, never sniffed or framed.
A per-caller cap on concurrent downloads; beyond it, 429.

nodes.title: /api/admin/*
nodes.text: The operational routes. Admin role only.
points: Disable hides a record from users without touching the CMS.
Requeue puts a failed batch (or a set-aside asset) back in line.
The queue report is what an operator watches.

nodes.title: Accept
nodes.text: Validates each event on its own, so one bad event never spoils the rest, then stores the whole batch and every accepted event in a single transaction before answering.
points: Each rule has a stable reason code (invalid_version, payload_too_large, timestamp_in_future…).
The payload is checksummed in a canonical form so the same content always has the same checksum.
Answered only after the commit: an acknowledgement means it is safely on disk.

nodes.title: Asset intake
nodes.text: Streams the bytes straight to disk (never held in memory), assembles multipart parts, verifies sizes and checksums, and enforces the store's quota before accepting anything.
points: A file is not served until it has been scanned.
Identical content is stored once.

nodes.title: Read queries
nodes.text: Reads through a separate, read-only database context. What a caller may see is decided here, from their role, never from a request parameter.
points: Users: published and not disabled. Admins: everything, with a status block.
Keyset pagination: stable under inserts, constant cost per page.

nodes.title: Asset serving
nodes.text: Looks the asset up and serves it only if its state is clean. Quarantined, rejected and set-aside assets are the same 404 as a missing one.
points: Range requests are handled by the framework's file streaming (206, 416, If-Range).
A range in an unknown unit is ignored (RFC 9110).

nodes.title: Admin services
nodes.text: The operational actions. Each writes an audit row in the same transaction as the change.
points: Delete of an asset overwrites the bytes with zeros before removing the file (best effort on SSDs and copy-on-write filesystems).

nodes.title: Queue and ledger
nodes.text: One table is both the work queue and the permanent record of every event received, so what was received is never in doubt.
points: Indexed so the worker's "next batch" is a seek, not a scan.
The queue has a size cap; a full queue answers 429 and stores nothing.
A failed batch is set aside (never retried forever, never dropped) until an admin requeues it.

nodes.title: Quarantine
nodes.text: Where every upload waits. Nothing here can be downloaded. A flagged file is wiped from here and only its verdict is kept.
points: Parts of unfinished multipart uploads live beside it and expire.

nodes.title: Current state
nodes.text: The latest state of every record, plus a payload-free tombstone for each deleted id so an older event can never bring it back.
points: secure_delete is on for every connection, so a deleted payload is overwritten in the file, not just unlinked.
WAL mode: readers never block the single writer.

nodes.title: Clean files
nodes.text: Cleared files, stored by the SHA-256 of their content, so identical files are stored once. A file reaches here only by an atomic move after a clean verdict.
points: Deleting the last asset that uses a blob removes the blob.

nodes.title: Audit log
nodes.text: Who did what to what, and when. Database triggers refuse any update or delete of a row, so history cannot be rewritten through this service.
points: Written in the same transaction as the action it records.
The test-only reset erases records but keeps the audit log.

nodes.title: Batch worker
nodes.text: A background worker that takes the oldest due batch and applies each event with a pure function: an event changes the stored state only if it sorts after it. The result does not depend on arrival order.
points: Replays and old versions are ignored, not applied twice.
Same version with different content: a deterministic winner, flagged as a conflict.
On failure it retries with back-off, then sets the batch aside; a poisoned batch never blocks the ones behind it.
A takedown (unpublish or delete) batch is retried forever, never set aside: the item stays visible until it applies, so it must apply.

nodes.title: Scan worker
nodes.text: Scans quarantined files outside the write lock, then in one transaction records the verdict. Clean: atomic move into the blob store. Infected or suspicious: wipe and keep only the verdict.
points: Fails closed: a scanner error or timeout leaves the file quarantined, retries with back-off, then sets it aside (still unserved).
The scanner sits behind an interface: a real engine such as ClamAV replaces the mock without changing the pipeline.
The mock is not malware protection; it proves the pipeline.

nodes.title: Sweeper
nodes.text: Housekeeping: abandoned multipart uploads expire, and files no row accounts for (stray parts, temp files, orphan blobs) are removed after a grace period.
points: It never takes a young file or one that is accounted for.

nodes.title: Everywhere: structured logs (never payloads or passwords) · metrics (queue depth, oldest age, failed bytes) · correlation ids · every call repeatable as curl
nodes.text: What lets an operator trust and debug the service.
points: Logs carry batch ids, counts and reason codes, never a payload, a password or an Authorization header.
Metrics include the queue depth and the age of the oldest waiting batch: a queue that quietly falls behind is the main risk of asynchronous processing.

steps.text: The CMS publishes, unpublishes or deletes something and POSTs a batch of events to the webhook.
The webhook checks who is calling (only the CMS account may) and the declared size, before reading any of the body.
Each event is validated on its own with a stable reason code, and the payload is checksummed in a canonical form.
The whole batch and every accepted event are stored in one transaction. Only then does the CMS get its answer: 202, with where to follow it.
A background worker takes the batch and applies each event with a pure function. Replays, old versions and late events change nothing.
The record's latest state (or a tombstone, for a delete) is written in the same transaction that marks the batch completed.
Later, a user reads the record. What they may see is decided by their role: users see published and enabled records; admins see everything.
The CMS uploads a file: one PUT, or multipart parts sent in parallel. Each part can carry a SHA-256 that is checked.
The bytes are streamed to disk, never held in memory. Sizes, checksums and the quota are checked.
The file waits in quarantine. Nothing here can be downloaded: a user asking for it gets the same 404 as for a file that does not exist.
The scan worker asks the scanner. If it errors or times out the file stays quarantined and is retried: fail closed.
Clean: the file is moved atomically into the content-addressed store. Infected: wiped, and only the verdict is kept.
Only now can a user download it, with byte ranges, so many ranges of a big file can be fetched in parallel and a download resumed.
An admin signs in. Admin routes are closed to every other role.
They hide a record, requeue a failed batch, re-scan an asset or delete one. Each action does one thing and checks its own preconditions.
Every action is recorded in the audit log in the same transaction as the change. The log cannot be updated or deleted through this service.
